summary:
Bremen stands under the national framework of Germany. The Self-Determination Act (SBGG) passed the Bundestag by 374 votes to 251 and took effect on 1 November 2024. Adults over 18 may change their legal gender by self-declaration, without the former medical or court pathway, and the change is entered in the civil registry through offices including Bremen's own. Bremen has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series of its own: the city-state's registry offices process declarations under the unchanged federal act, and federal criminal law and the General Act on Equal Treatment apply without local deviation.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prison administration is a Land competence and Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so the national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions. All Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender, and § 6(1) SBGG permits state law to override the registry entry. Many Länder have enacted exception clauses under that provision, some abstract and framed as applying to all inmates, others criticised as directed specifically at trans prisoners.

The exception has produced outcomes in both directions. In the Liebich case, covered by France24 on 16 July 2026, a neo-Nazi prisoner was held in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change. The case drove Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, a proposal that would alter the framework Bremen applies if it succeeds.

Same-sex marriage has been legal throughout Germany, and therefore in Bremen, since 1 October 2017.
tangentialFactors:
Prison administration and civil registry offices are Land competences across Germany, so Bremen's position on placement and gender-entry processing tracks the federal framework rather than diverging from it. The Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 reads this national layer as the standard Bremen operates under, and records that the Länder have responded to the Self-Determination Act unevenly, with exception clauses of differing breadth.

The political turbulence is federal rather than local. The Bundesrat initiative launched by Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia after the Liebich reporting is an attempt to tighten the national act itself, which would bind Bremen's registry offices and courts without any Bremen legislative step. A visitor should therefore treat Bremen's current position as contingent on federal proceedings in a way that a city-state statute would not be.
localsOnly:
Bremen's registry offices process gender-entry declarations under the unchanged federal act, with no local form, waiting period or medical requirement of their own beyond the three months' notice the Self-Determination Act provides. Residents of Bremen have no local ordinance to appeal to on the question, and their remedy lies in the federal act and federal administrative routes.

Residents of Bremen held in custody fall under the national placement framework because the city-state has enacted no placement statute. The practical consequence is that a Bremen prisoner's housing follows legal gender as the default, subject to whatever exception clause the applicable prison legislation contains, and Bremen offers no locally enacted protection against that override.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006, and that protection applies in Bremen without local modification. A nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has been in force since May 2020, carrying penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bremen-specific prison-placement decision, complaint or enforcement record is documented in the sources reviewed. Whether Bremen's prison service has issued guidance for trans detainees, as Berlin's has, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The sources do not itemise which Länder's exception clauses are abstract and which are criticised as trans-targeted, and they do not state whether any of those clauses governs a Bremen facility. That mapping is unresolved.

No data is available on how long Bremen's registry offices take to process declarations, whether they have refused any, or whether residents have challenged a refusal. Processing practice in Bremen is not sourced.

The Bundesrat initiative by Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia is reported as launched; its passage and its effect on the federal Self-Determination Act are not established in the sources and remain unresolved.

German criminal-law history under Section 175, including the Nazi-era tightening of Section 175a and the persecution of men in custody, carries no trans-specific bearing on a visitor's present exposure and is not carried into this record.
